Think about 1996-2006 and then 2006 to 2016. Even more so the last 5 years (2011-2016). It feels as though things haven't changed much in the last 5 years. A computer made in 2006 would be obsolete in 2011 but a computer from 2011 would still be alright today for example (I would actually recommend buying a used pc from the early 2010s to save a lot of money and maybe do some minor upgrades). What do you think?

Advancements today are mostly in the intelligence and "back of the system" improvements rather than forward facing consumer stuff. You don't notice when the power grid gets more efficient, or your search results are better tuned, but they are improving just as fast as they always have been.

You're looking at the flat top of the integrated circuit s curve combined with an economic down-turn, a pause as technologies are integrated and repackaged (smart phones, VR, infrastructure and social building methods, a revolution in management, new manufacturing techniques... all important foundations for what comes next) and a global marketplace taking a breather after an upheaval.

But here's the thing: integrated circuits took four times as long as previous physical information technologies to stop improving. During that time we've had four times as long to consider alternatives. Chemistry and physics have undergone a revolution in that time.The changes that are coming will be a tsunami to the kiddy pool splash of the last 30 years.
We are getting to the refinement stage of computers now. It's not slower, just harder to see.

I've commented on Steam Machines and SteamOS a number of times and always get piled on for saying almost exactly what that article does. They're a failure. Why are they a failure? Because there is no real or perceived deficiency in Windows as a gaming platform. Of course there are other reasons, but that is the biggest and most important. Gaming on Windows is pretty rock solid. If you're trying to entice people to purchase an (expensive and non-competitively priced) new gaming computer that runs an unfamiliar OS, you better be offering a compelling incentive. There is none. Worse yet, Steam Machines are primarily marketed to compete with consoles (living room use with a controller). PC gamers, which make up the vast majority of Steam users, aren't looking for a console.

I could go on with more examples of how Steam Machines and Steam OS were a fool's errand, but instead let me just remind everyone that they were born out of a hissy fit that Gabe Newell had when he learned that Microsoft was going to be competing with Steam by opening their own store. Steam has LONG dominated sales on PCs, having a near virtual monopoly. Gabe's "Plan B" was to try to drag PC gamers away from Windows and onto a fork of Linux where he could basically create a walled-garden.

Lots of folks on Voat hate Microsoft/Windows and lots of folks here love Linux...but this isn't even about that. Steam Machines and Steam OS are now, and will continue to be, a failure. Last time I checked, Steam on Linux represented around 1% of all Steam use. 99% of PC gamers have zero complaints with Windows as a gaming platform, and they will not pay money to "upgrade" to a console experience that is less capable than their current rigs.

a fork of Linux where he could basically create a walled-garden.

This sentence makes literally no sense.

Why is that? Forks of Linux exist. Forks are free to add proprietary elements. A forked version can be commercially developed in order to keep competitors off the platform or make it extremely difficult for the average user to do so. Just look at Fire OS, a fork of Android (which is a version of Linux). Amazon's Fire OS is mostly compatible with Google's Android, but they don't allow the use of Google Services or GAPPs unless you root (which few users do).
EDIT:
I'd add that the vision of SteamOS is much more in the vein of FireOS. The whole "Big Picture" mode (the default) is tied directly to the Steam Store. FireOS devices are pretty much the same--the Amazon Store is EVERYWHERE. I'm happy to explain myself, but it is unnecessarily in the weeds (and not central to the issue at hand). Have you used SteamOS? The GUI is the store. You boot up in Big Screen mode, and just like FireOS, your entire GUI is basically a storefront selling you stuff exclusively from Steam. Steam is all-in on DRM too. They're not in the Linux game because they they software should be free. They're 100% involved with Linux because they're looking for a platform that they can control and monopolize. Look at how they attempted to start charging for gaming mods--stuff that had a decades long history of being free--Steam came in and schemed a way to lock it down and tried to start charging for it.
